AED choice must account for reproductive age, occupation, and adherence in a busy worker.

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Chanthavong is a 19-year-old left-handed female restaurant worker who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred at home earlier today. Her partner reports that they were preparing dinner together when the patient suddenly stopped what she was doing, appeared to stare blankly ahead, and began making chewing movements with her jaw while her left hand picked repetitively at her apron. He called her name repeatedly but she did not respond. After approximately 20 seconds of this behavior, her body stiffened and she fell to the floor, followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs lasting roughly 60 to 90 seconds. She was briefly cyanotic around her lips during the convulsive phase. She bit her tongue during the event. There was no urinary incontinence. Afterward, she was confused and unable to speak coherently for approximately 20 minutes, then gradually became drowsy and fell asleep for about two hours before arriving at the emergency department.

On interview, the patient reports that just before the episode she perceived a strong, unpleasant smell that she describes as something like burning rubber, accompanied by a wave of nausea rising from her abdomen into her chest. She recalls nothing after that until waking up feeling exhausted and sore. She further reports that she has experienced similar episodes of perceiving a foul smell followed by nausea and a feeling of detachment approximately five to six times over the past eight months. These episodes would last 30 to 90 seconds and resolve spontaneously, leaving her feeling briefly disoriented. On two occasions, coworkers noticed her staring and being unresponsive for a short period, but she dismissed these as stress-related episodes. She has never previously sought medical attention for these events. She denies any recent head trauma, febrile illness, sleep deprivation beyond her normal schedule, or medication changes. She has no history of meningitis or encephalitis. She reports drinking one glass of wine the evening prior to the seizure, which is within her normal pattern.
